Executive Summary

Premium ARR multiples go to teams that can prove durable ARR growth. Most can't.

I've worked on over 25+ multi-billion-dollar Tech M&A deals during my time at PwC, and in every one, a CFO or CEO said something to the effect of, "Interesting, I wish I knew that a year ago." A CFO of a $100M ARR health care software business even told me, "I spent a million dollars on a data team and software, and they weren't able to provide these insights." So why the imbalance? Why do acquirers get to know a company's ARR faster and better than the company itself?

It's simple: Buy-side diligence teams are paid a lot of money to uncover insights during diligence, and it's all they do. Finance, RevOps, and Data & Analytics teams are paid good enough money to take care of daily, weekly, and monthly operating tasks. These internal teams focused on operations don't have a chance compared to deal teams. They don't have the M&A experience, and they don't have the capacity (time) to provide M&A-grade insights to their company leadership team and board. The result: companies are stuck choosing to spend half a million dollars on Big 4 sell-side support or get hit with multi-million dollar haircuts on the purchase price.

There is a third option boards, operating partners, and management teams should be aware of: AI-enabled M&A advisors. Big 4 experienced M&A advisors who have created purpose-built AI platforms and AI agents for due diligence to support companies grinding through the day-to-day operations. Pacer AI provides Quality of Revenue insights and has partnered with Veach.AI for Quality of Earnings and Commercial Due Diligence. Additionally, we've partnered with Weighbridge for Technical Due Diligence.

Partner with Pacer AI to get the Big 4, M&A-grade insights while you're operating your business, not just during diligence.

1. Situation

Four Questions Boards & CFOs Should Be Able to Answer

Most management teams can answer these anecdotally. Few can answer them with data.

1. Can you explain the drivers of your ARR growth, and how you have accelerated them?

Is growth driven through NRR improvements or by acquiring more customers? Is growth tailwind-driven or operationally driven through operational rigor, playbooks, and systems?

2. Which cohorts drive NRR and why?

Is net retention strong across all vintage years, or is it dropping in more recent years? How come? Are NRR challenges market-based? Industry-based? Both?

3. How have you improved your upsell and cross-sell rates?

Can you show expansion decomposed into upsell, cross-sell, and price increase? Can you demonstrate improvement over time by segment?

4. What drives churn, and what is your strategy to mitigate it?

Is churn product driven? Is it concentrated by market, segment or account size? Where have you identified churn trends and mitigated them?

After every question, acquirers will ask: how much whitespace is there to sell into?

Bonus Points Question

How much whitespace is there to sell into?
Being able to clearly explain (a) obtainable whitespace at the market level by segment and vertical, (b) key accounts whitespace, and (c) expansion whitespace at the account level (upsell, cross-sell, price increase) supports your target valuation.

2. Complication

The Experience Gap

There is a significant experience gap between what the board wants and the capability to provide it.

Combined M&A Experience

An example of cumulative number of M&A transactions experienced

Portfolio Company
5
Board
25+

Teams will often take the approach they do with other problems: try a DIY solution in Excel or a BI tool, or buy a SaaS solution, or try to build an ARR Snowball with Claude. Approaching this problem as a technical challenge is the incorrect approach. This is not about building an output; it's about how you present and talk about your business internally or to potential acquirers, which requires expertise from someone who has done it in due diligence and for operational improvements.

Board-quality ARR analysis is about "Quality of Revenue."

Quality of Revenue diligence occurs with recurring revenue businesses to identify how durable the ARR growth is. A company with durable ARR growth has at least 1/3 of the growth coming from the customer base — i.e., a company with 15% ARR growth and 5% of the 15% coming from NRR gains. A company without durable ARR growth is often experiencing a significant leaky bucket where the customers they acquire don't expand or aren't retained very long, impacting CaC payback and cash flow. Understanding "Quality of Revenue" diligence provides the perspective to decide why to optimize for GRR or NRR and the ability to explain to stakeholders and acquirers.

Companies that decide to focus on NRR to make their growth more durable often discuss creating an expansion division. These types of operational and organizational discussions require their own depth of understanding around compensation, rep-to-account ratios, and expansion enablement requirements. The Pacer AI team has the experience and resources to support these conversations as well.

The technical aspect of creating ARR Snowballs, a standard Quality of Revenue output in diligence, is only about 1/3 of the challenge. The other two-thirds are a mix of (a) term alignment: term definitions, sources, and calculations, and (b) commercial knowledge and experience to advise stakeholders on how to present and message ARR performance as well as operationally improve it.

What got you here won't get you there.

The Excel approach — where most teams start.

Excel doesn't scale to complexity or the data size well. Prone to error, challenging to get upsell & cross-sell visibility. Cohort analysis is very difficult.

The database approach

Better structure, scales better, and is more customizable, but still requires expertise to architect and present.

The SaaS tool approach

Built to scale their own customers with a one-size-fits-all approach. Customization is limited and challenging. Prioritizes presentation over perspective.

3. Complexity

The Data Architecture Gap

"Trust in God, All Others Bring Data" — Edwards Deming

In diligence, every large ARR movement and anecdotal story will be audited in the customer data cube, see the example below. The customer data cube is the foundation for an M&A-grade ARR Snowball. Building it requires expertise into a number of critical questions.

The Customer Data Cube — account-product granularity with upsell, cross-sell, and revenue motion callouts

Critical Questions

Architecture Questions

Building an ARR Snowball is like designing a software user interface. There is already an end design in mind, but you have to architect an underlying database to ensure the accuracy of the user interface.

Often, the hardest part is aligning definitions across the company. A common challenge is explaining that booked ARR is not reported ARR due to ASC 606. Another common confusion, especially for Salesforce CRM users, is around "Expansion." Salesforce CRMs often have an "Expansion Opportunity," which can cause disagreement between Sales and Finance on the Expansion ARR reported vs what's in Salesforce. This is especially challenging for the Sales and RevOps team, who have been trained that Salesforce or HubSpot is the source of truth.

What is the purpose?
  • Planning: Forecasting, Territory, Scenario planning, etc.
  • Reporting: Daily flash, MBR, QBR, Board
  • Strategic: Optimize for NRR or GRR?
What level of granularity?
  • Account Level: $100 on Acct 1001
  • Account-Product Level: $100 on Acct 1001 from $70 with Product A and $30 with Product B
  • Account-Product-<wrinkle> (e.g., on-prem vs. cloud)
What sources will we use?
  • Bookings: CRM (Salesforce, HubSpot, etc.) or contract database
  • Billings: Stripe or other online payment platforms
  • Reported Revenue: ERPs like NetSuite, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks
What do we reconcile to?
  • Period: Most recent period displayed
  • Bookings: Total ACV
  • Billings: Total invoice amount
  • Revenue: Reported recurring revenue

Presentation Questions

Deciding what and how to present is not straightforward. Most companies have hierarchies of accounts (Parent, Child) and products (SKU, product, product category). The most common course of action is to present as you operate the business.

Why is it not straightforward? A common situation is when a company defines new account ARR as ARR from acquiring a new child account. However, when displaying the ARR Snowball at a child account level, churn will be higher as opposed to deciding to use the parent account as the account level "unit of analysis." Understanding these second and third-order effects is critical. An experienced Quality of Revenue M&A advisor will help position the company for premium valuation and optimize the customer data cube architecture to be able to show multiple potential views of the ARR Snowball.

What periods?
  • Monthly: Display ARR with 12-month look back, or MRR
  • Quarterly: Quarterly ARR annualized with 3-month look back, or ARR with 12-month look back
  • Annual
What account level?
  • Child Account — optimizes for New ARR and customer count, but could increase churn
  • Parent Account — increases upsell and NRR but decreases New ARR
  • Ultimate Parent Account — increases upsell and NRR but decreases New ARR and customer count
What product level?
  • SKU — increases cross-sell but can increase product churn too
  • Product
  • Product group
  • Product line — decreases cross-sell, increases upsell, but could increase downsell

— see next page for The Good, the Bad, the Unhelpful —

4. Overview

The Good, the Bad, the Unhelpful,
and what M&A-Grade looks like

A basic > intermediate > advanced framework to understand the three levels of ARR Snowball analytics.

The Good (but not M&A-grade yet)

A good ARR Snowball analysis provides:

  • ✓ A multi-period view using an ARR Waterfall framework
  • ✓ Ending ARR is equal to the sum of the ARR movements
  • ✓ The period rolls — the end of one period equals the beginning of the next period
  • ✓ An analysis of ARR based on movements as a percentage of beginning
  • ✓ Renewal visibility, customer type breakdown

This view also provides insights into renewal performance and a breakdown of newly acquired customers into true New, current customers that lapsed on their renewal, and a returning customer (winback) that hasn't been a customer in more than 12 months.

The Good — multi-period view with renewal insights and % of beginning analysis

The Bad

A basic ARR Snowball checks some boxes but falls short on the analysis that matters. It often leaves users thinking, "ok, what do I do with this?" This basic ARR Snowball table often comes from ARR Roll-Forward forecast modeling. It signals the company has the knowledge to understand an ARR Waterfall, but doesn't have the experience to know what right looks like.

  • ✓ A multi-period view using an ARR Waterfall framework
  • ✓ Ending ARR is equal to the sum of the ARR movements
  • ✓ The period rolls — the end of one period equals the beginning of the next period
  • × An analysis of ARR based on movements as a percentage of beginning
  • × Renewal visibility, customer type breakdown
The Bad — account-level only, no % of beginning, no renewal breakdown, cannot explain drivers

The Unhelpful

The most common ARR visual in board decks checks almost none of the boxes:

  • × A multi-period view using an ARR Waterfall framework
  • ✓ Ending ARR is equal to the sum of the ARR movements
  • × The period rolls — the end of one period equals the beginning of the next period
  • × An analysis of ARR based on movements as a percentage of beginning
  • × Renewal visibility, customer type breakdown
The Unhelpful — waterfall bridge charts prioritize presentation over perspective

What M&A-Grade Looks Like

M&A-grade Advanced ARR Snowballs check every box and go further — providing at account-product granularity with nine or more ARR movement categories, which can be applied by market, by segment, by vintage, and by cohort (market-segment, segment-account size). Most importantly, reconciled back to the financial statements.

M&A-Grade — account-product granularity, 9+ movements, vintage & cohort cuts, reconciled to financials

Vintage Analysis example

Net Retention by Vintage Year

Gross Retention by Vintage Year

5. The Question

How Can We Deliver Diligence-Grade Insights to the Board?

Building an M&A-grade ARR Snowball requires coordination across multiple teams — each with their own priorities and existing workloads:

Finance Team
  • CFO as the project sponsor
  • VP of FP&A as the project owner
  • Verifies accuracy
  • Needs data and analytics support
RevOps Team
  • Cleanses data
  • Verifies account hierarchies
  • Verifies product hierarchies
Data Team
  • Compiles the data
  • Builds the database model
Analytics Team
  • Builds the presentation model
  • Builds the dimensional analytics cuts
  • Builds the vintage analytics cuts

Don't attempt an in-house "DIY" build unless you have a person who has built multiple ARR Snowballs before for boards or for due diligence.

A DIY build typically takes 6+ people, 6+ months.
For companies over $100M ARR it often takes 10+ months.

— see next page for ARR Snowball reporting roadmap —

6. The Journey

ARR Snowball Reporting Roadmap

The path from current state to M&A-grade is a progression: Basic to Intermediate to Advanced. Each level unlocks new operational insights: Renewal, Expansion drivers, Contraction drivers, and the win-backs cohort of New ARR.

Basic → Intermediate → Advanced — each level unlocks new operational insights
Advanced ARR Snowball Formula
BoP − Churn − Product Churn − Downsell − Contraction + Upsell + Cross-sell + New + Lapsed + Returning = EoP
Advanced models provide both operational and strategic clarity — Basic provides neither

— see next page for Options: Build, Buy, Big 4, AI Enabled —

Building an M&A-grade ARR Snowball requires coordination across multiple teams — each with their own priorities and existing workloads:

Finance Team
  • CFO as the project sponsor
  • VP of FP&A as the project owner
  • Verifies accuracy
  • Needs data and analytics support
RevOps Team
  • Cleanses data
  • Verifies account hierarchies
  • Verifies product hierarchies
Data Team
  • Compiles the data
  • Builds the database model
Analytics Team
  • Builds the presentation model
  • Builds the dimensional analytics cuts
  • Builds the vintage analytics cuts

Don’t attempt an in-house “DIY” build unless you have a person who has built multiple ARR Snowballs before for boards or for due diligence.

A DIY build typically takes 6+ people, 6+ months.
For companies over $100M ARR it often takes 10+ months.

— see next page for ARR Snowball reporting roadmap —

6. The Journey

ARR Snowball Reporting Roadmap

The path from current state to M&A-grade is a progression: Basic to Intermediate to Advanced. Each level unlocks new operational insights: Renewal, Expansion drivers, Contraction drivers, and the win-backs cohort of New ARR.

Basic → Intermediate → Advanced — each level unlocks new operational insights
Advanced ARR Snowball Formula
BoP − Churn − Product Churn − Downsell − Contraction + Upsell + Cross-sell + New + Lapsed + Returning = EoP
Advanced models provide both operational and strategic clarity — Basic provides neither
